analysis.one_liner: Lets bank customers stop their bank from sharing or selling their personal financial information.
analysis.headline: Despite 20 cosponsors, the bill never left the House Banking Committee — it was referred to a subcommittee in June 1999 and died when the 106th Congress ended without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required banks, bank holding companies, and their affiliates to give customers a clear, separate privacy notice and let customers opt out — by mail, email, or fax — before the bank shared or sold the customer's personal financial information to anyone else, including the bank's own affiliates. It carved out exceptions for ordinary transactions like processing checks, dealing with regulators, courts, and debt collectors, and fighting fraud. It never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank and financial-services customers, who would gain the right to keep their account balances, transactions, and personal details from being shared or sold without their say-so. The bill also required a standalone 'Privacy Notice' in prominent type, mailed separately, so customers could not miss it.

how_it_helps.text: Banks, bank holding companies, and their affiliates could not disclose or transfer personally identifiable customer information — transactions, balances, payout dates — to any other person, including their own affiliates, unless the customer had been notified and had not opted out [S3].

The privacy notice had to be a separate document with 'Privacy Notice' in prominent type, mailed separately from any other statement, and acknowledged separately if given in person, so it could not be buried in junk mail [S3].
Customers could opt out in writing at any time, including by email or fax, and a 30-day window after notice blocked sharing so customers had a real chance to respond [S3].

Everyday banking was preserved: exceptions allowed sharing to process transactions the customer authorized, clear checks, report to regulators and courts, work with credit bureaus and debt collectors, and prevent fraud [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, bank holding companies, and their affiliates, which would lose the ability to freely share and sell customer data across their corporate families and to outside marketers, and would bear the cost of preparing and mailing separate privacy notices and honoring opt-outs.

drawbacks.text: The bill used an opt-out system, not opt-in: banks could share customer data unless the customer affirmatively objected, so customers who never mailed back a form would still have their information shared [S3].

Banks and their affiliates would bear compliance costs — producing separate privacy notices, tracking written opt-outs by mail, email, and fax — and would lose revenue from cross-marketing and data-sharing within their corporate families [S3].
Some customers value the convenience of affiliated companies offering them integrated products based on shared information, which this bill would restrict along with unwanted sharing [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy protections are real and the exceptions are sensibly drawn — routine transactions, regulators, courts, and fraud prevention all keep working. The main design weakness is the opt-out mechanism: a customer has to take action to stop the sharing, and many will not, so the protection is stronger in theory than in practice. The compliance burden on banks is real but modest. On balance the bill trades a modest bank cost for a meaningful customer right.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking Committee and then to its subcommittee on financial institutions, and sat there until the 106th Congress ended without ever getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jay Inslee introduced the bill on May 25, 1999, and it was referred to the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services the same day [S5].
On June 11, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, where no further action followed [S5].
Inslee made introductory remarks again in May 2000, but the bill never advanced to a markup or a floor vote [S5].
The bill drew 20 cosponsors — 19 Democrats and 1 Independent — but no member of the House majority brought it forward, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and financial conglomerates came out ahead: they kept the ability to share and sell customer financial information freely, since no competing privacy bill became law instead.

for.name: Rep. Jay Inslee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the House floor in 1999 and again in 2000 seeking to advance it.

for.name: Rep. Paul Kanjorski
for.role: Cosponsor (D-PA), member of the House Banking Committee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, lending support from inside the committee to which it was referred.

for.name: 20 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, 19 Democrats and 1 Independent, but included no Republicans.

against.name: Rep. Jim Leach
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Banking and Financial Services
against.what_they_did: The committee to which the bill was referred took it no further than subcommittee referral; no markup was ever scheduled and the bill never reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders; no Republican supported the bill, and the Republican-chaired committee never moved it.

industries.note: The bill would have ended free sharing and sale of customer account data across a banking company and its affiliates, a practice that drives cross-marketing revenue. Banks' gain from unrestricted data sharing comes directly at the expense of customers' control over their own financial information.
The bill restricted banks from transferring customer data to outside persons for marketing, cutting off a channel these firms use to reach bank customers with targeted offers.
